eras.name: Iron and Steam
eras.cost: Steam made Britain rich and its towns black with soot. Factories pulled people off the land, and the handloom weavers were undercut by the power loom.

gadget.name: Steam Whistle
gadget.text: One blast and the weaker wild creatures keep clear for 100 steps, like a Lavender Sachet. Once a day.

eras.name: Sparks and Wires
eras.cost: Prices, orders and news began to move at the speed of electricity, and so did the running of an empire. Telegraph clerks and messenger boys found work, until the telephone came for theirs.

gadget.name: Telegraph Office
gadget.text: Wire money from wherever you are: the bureau de change, at its own rates, without the walk.

eras.name: Airwaves and Atoms
eras.cost: Radar helped win the Battle of Britain. Television emptied the cinemas, whose audiences fell steeply through the 1950s. Splitting the atom gave us power stations, and the bomb.

gadget.name: Pocket Wireless
gadget.text: The Shipping Forecast for the nearest sea, and how long this weather has left, wherever you stand.

eras.name: Thinking Machines
eras.cost: Rooms of human computers, often women doing sums by hand, were replaced by machines. Bletchley's codebreakers, most of them women, kept their secret for some thirty years.

gadget.name: The Reckoner
gadget.text: Counts the plaques here you haven't read yet, and points you at the nearest one.

eras.name: The Networked Isles
eras.cost: The web put the world's libraries in your pocket, and its rumours too. Bank branches, travel agents and record shops closed; coders, app makers and delivery riders appeared.

gadget.name: The Web
gadget.text: Look up where the creatures you've seen but not yet caught are said to live.

eras.name: Learning Machines
eras.cost: AI helps read scans, translate and find new medicines. It also uses a great deal of electricity, copies the faults in its examples and can be wrong with total confidence. Some jobs change or go. What it is for is still ours to decide.

gadget.name: Field Guide Model
gadget.text: Guesses what you'll meet here, learnt only from your own sightings. Often right. Not always.

entries.title: Boyle's Law
entries.text: Robert Boyle, born at Lismore Castle in County Waterford, showed that a gas squeezed into half the space pushes back twice as hard.
entries.where: A plaque in the Comeraghs, County Waterford

entries.title: The Iron Bridge
entries.text: Cast at Coalbrookdale and put up over the Severn in 1779: the first major bridge in the world made of cast iron.
entries.cost: The gorge ran on coal: smoke and slag heaps by day, furnace glow by night.

entries.title: Dalton's Atoms
entries.text: John Dalton, a Quaker teacher in Manchester, argued that every element is made of its own kind of atom, with its own weight.

entries.title: The Safety Lamp
entries.text: Humphry Davy, from Penzance, wrapped a miner's flame in fine wire gauze so it could not set off the gas in a pit.
entries.cost: It saved lives, and it also let mine owners send men into gassier seams.

entries.title: Stephenson's Rocket
entries.text: The Stephensons' Rocket won the Rainhill Trials in October 1829 at nearly 30 miles an hour.
entries.where: Chat Moss, or the Stephensons' works in Newcastle
entries.cost: Stagecoaches and coaching inns lost their trade within a generation; the railways became one of Britain's biggest employers.

entries.title: Faraday's Dynamo
entries.text: Michael Faraday moved a magnet through a coil of wire and made electricity flow. Every power station still does the same trick.

entries.title: The Electric Telegraph
entries.text: William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented their telegraph in 1837. News that took a day by horse now took minutes.

entries.title: Light Is a Wave
entries.text: James Clerk Maxwell's equations tied electricity, magnetism and light together, and predicted the invisible waves we now call radio.

entries.title: The Atlantic Cable
entries.text: A lasting telegraph cable ran from Valentia Island in Kerry to Newfoundland in 1866. A message that took about ten days by ship took minutes.

entries.title: Radio Across the Atlantic
entries.text: On 12 December 1901 Guglielmo Marconi said he heard the Morse letter S in Newfoundland, sent from Poldhu in Cornwall.
entries.cost: Ships at sea could call for help at last.

entries.title: Television
entries.text: John Logie Baird, from Helensburgh, showed moving television pictures in an attic in Soho on 26 January 1926.

entries.title: The Flat Benzene Ring
entries.text: Kathleen Lonsdale, from Newbridge in County Kildare, used X-rays to prove that the benzene ring is flat.

entries.title: Splitting the Atom
entries.text: Ernest Walton, from Dungarvan, and John Cockcroft split lithium atoms with a beam of protons in Cambridge.
entries.where: A plaque in the Comeraghs, County Waterford

entries.title: Radar
entries.text: Radio echoes off an RAF bomber were picked up near Daventry in 1935; by 1939 the Chain Home stations watched the coast.

entries.title: The Jet Engine
entries.text: Frank Whittle's first jet engine ran on a test bed in Rugby in April 1937. A jet first flew in Britain in 1941.

entries.title: The Double Helix
entries.text: Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 was the vital clue when Watson and Crick worked out the double helix of DNA in 1953.
entries.where: Cambridge, or the lab at Roslin

entries.title: The Lovell Telescope
entries.text: Jodrell Bank's giant dish in Cheshire was finished in 1957, in time to track the rocket that carried Sputnik.

entries.title: Lovelace's Notes
entries.text: Ada Lovelace set out, step by step, how Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine could work out a sequence of numbers: a program, a century early.

entries.title: The Bombe
entries.text: Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman's Bombe raced through Enigma's possible settings to find each day's key.

entries.title: Colossus
entries.text: Tommy Flowers' Colossus, the first programmable electronic digital computer, was reading Lorenz messages at Bletchley by early 1944.

entries.title: The Manchester Baby
entries.text: On 21 June 1948 the Baby ran the first program ever held in a computer's own electronic memory.

entries.title: Can Machines Think?
entries.text: Working in Manchester, Turing asked in 1950 whether a machine could think, and proposed a test: could it pass for a person in conversation?

entries.title: The First Pulsar
entries.text: Jocelyn Bell Burnell, from Lurgan, spotted a tiny, regular blip on her radio telescope's chart: a spinning dead star.

entries.title: The ARM Chip
entries.text: Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber's frugal ARM processor first ran at Acorn in Cambridge. Its descendants are in nearly every phone.

entries.title: The First Mobile Call
entries.text: On New Year's Day 1985 Ernie Wise made the first public mobile phone call in Britain, from St Katharine Docks.

entries.title: The World Wide Web
entries.text: Tim Berners-Lee, from London, proposed the web at CERN in March 1989, and it was given to the world free.

entries.title: The Raspberry Pi
entries.text: A bare 35 dollar computer the size of a credit card, from a Cambridge charity, to get young people tinkering again.

entries.title: AlphaGo
entries.text: DeepMind's AlphaGo, from London, beat Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players alive, by four games to one.

entries.title: AlphaFold
entries.text: Having learnt from about 170,000 protein shapes found by scientists, AlphaFold could predict new ones, often nearly as well as the lab.
entries.cost: Its makers Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared in the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the lab scientists' 170,000 shapes made it possible.

entries.title: AI in Plain Words
entries.text: A model learns patterns from examples. It can be wrong, it copies the faults of its examples, and people still have to check it and decide.
entries.where: Dr Rao, by King's Cross Station, London
